## Assistant
A **snapshot** is a frozen copy of state at one moment, so you can look back or restore without depending on whatever changed later.

**What people usually mean**

- **Disks / VMs:** a point-in-time image of a volume or machine (AWS EBS, Hyper-V, VirtualBox). Roll back if an upgrade fails.
- **Filesystems:** cheap copy-on-write views (ZFS, btrfs, APFS). New writes go elsewhere; the snapshot still shows the old tree.
- **Databases:** a consistent backup of tables at time T (Postgres `pg_dump`, filesystem freeze + copy).
- **Code:** a tagged commit is a snapshot of the repo. Git is a chain of those.

The shared idea: **don’t only overwrite the live file.** Keep an immutable “this is what we believed at version N.”

**In this project**

`reports/versions/v7` … `v57` are interpretation snapshots. Live reports (`codex-originator-dashboard.md`, the spec, scores) can be updated. The `vN` folders keep the earlier reading so later agents don’t pretend v40’s numbers were always the story. CONTINUE’s rule is recode into versions, **do not only overwrite**.

**What a snapshot is not**

It is not a backup of the raw Codex JSONL (that stays hashed and gitignored). It is not a VM image of your PC. It is a dated, named copy of **analysis and spec**, so gold can change without erasing the trail.

data.text: I have enough to write a detailed, human explanation of what "don't act like it" means. This is a talk-to-user briefing. No more tools needed.

**“Don’t act like it” is about the sequence of moves, not about whether the English sounds smart.** Work, Kilo, and OpenCode can all *say* “I’ll look at the repo first.” Only Work actually *stops* there most of the time. Kilo and OpenCode still treat a coding chat as “read a bit, make a todo, then start editing.”

That is the whole gap. Same kind of user ask. Different muscle memory in the harness.

## What Work actually does

Imagine you ask Work something ordinary: “what’s going on in this project” or “fix this,” or even a multi-step job.

Work almost always starts by **looking**. In the transcripts that is `exec`: short inspect bursts, like reading cells. Median burst is **3** looks. It does **not** open a todo list. It does **not** start in the terminal. It does **not** spawn a helper as move one.

Then it usually does one of three things:

- **Stop.** About **35 of 87** Work sessions never write and never spawn. They looked, then answered. That is the default.
- **Wait.** About **31 of 83** nonempty sessions wait on a slow cell, then look again. After a wait, the next move is look — never patch.
- **Send.** About **25** sessions, after a long look (median **15** tools), hand a named slice to another worker. They send again later if needed. They almost never patch in between.

Patching is the exception: **1 session in 83**. Todo lists: **zero**. First tool is send: **zero**. First tool is a cwd shell: **2**.

So Work’s personality, in one line: **research is the job; changing files is rare.**

When we map those habits onto the scorer, Work itself passes **81 of 83** sessions. The exam is not fake. Work really does this.

## What Kilo actually does

Kilo *starts* like Work. On the 13 scored `code` sessions, **all 13 look first**. Zero write-first. That part is fine.

Then it diverges.

A typical Kilo coding chat looks like:

1. Read / glob / grep (good).
2. Pretty soon, **Todowrite** — a checklist. Work never does this. Median tools before Kilo’s first task/todo is **3**. Work waits until **15** before it even sends.
3. Then it **edits anyway**. **11 of 13** sessions write. Write-rate **0.85**. Work’s write-rate is about **0.01**.
4. After a burst of reading, the next move is often **edit**, not wait or send. That is the R5 fail. Work’s count for “look burst then patch” is **0**.

So you get this pattern, which showed up in **5 of 13** Kilo `code` sessions as the single most common fail mask: **look, todo, edit**.

What you would notice in the product: the agent sounds careful, it opens a lot of files (median **51** tools before the first write — it over-reads), then it still **mutates the tree**. Work would often have already answered without touching disk.

Kilo also **writes without sending a sub-task** in 11 of 13 sessions. Work’s multi-piece move is “send to a named worker after looking.” Kilo’s multi-piece move is “make a todo, then patch it yourself.”

Only **1 of 13** Kilo `code` sessions does the full Work loop. That is the **8%**.

## What OpenCode actually does

OpenCode’s extra habit is **bash first**.

On 21 scored sessions, **10 start in the shell**. Work starts in inspect **81** times and in a cwd shell **twice**. Three more OpenCode sessions start with Todowrite. Two start by spawning a task. One starts by writing.

Then the same Kilo problem: it still writes a lot (**write-rate 0.62**), still todos (**10 of 21**), still edits at the end of a look burst.

The most common OpenCode fail mask is **bash + todo + edit** (6 of 19 `build` sessions). Another 3 fail **only** because they opened the terminal first — they might look fine after that, but Work almost never starts that way.

Only **3 of 19** `build` sessions match. That is the **16%**.

What you would notice: OpenCode often “checks the machine” before it reads the files. Work reads first. OpenCode also likes a plan list. Work does not.

## What “act like it” would look like

If the copies acted like Work, a normal coding chat would look like this:

- First click is **read/search**, not terminal, not todo, not spawn.
- A short look burst, then either an answer, a wait, or a named handoff.
- **Most sessions never edit.** Editing is the exception, not the default “I am a coding agent so I patch.”
- If it does edit, it does **not** do it as the next move after a look burst. It waits or sends or stops, then looks again.
- No checklist tool. Multi-piece work is “send this slice to X,” not “here are 6 todos I will now implement.”

Kilo already does the first bullet. It fails the rest. OpenCode fails the first bullet too.

The Codex **mode file** already says those rules. Live `code` / `build` sessions still don’t follow them. Sqlite also never stored `agent=codex`, so we have been scoring the default coding agents — the copies people actually use — not a clean “Codex mode only” exam.

## What this is *not* saying

This is **not** “Grok is dumber than Codex” or “the patch they shipped was wrong.” We have not finished replaying the same 22 Work tickets into both products and grading the resulting files.

It is saying: **on chats they already ran, the harness still behaves like a write-happy coding agent, and Work does not.** That is the 8–16% versus 98%.
so how is our project planning to fix this exact thing?

The user wants to understand how the project plans to fix the gap - Kilo/OpenCode not acting like ChatGPT Work. I should look at the actual plan documents: PLAN.md, iteration-loop spec, ISSUES, matche...
I’ll read the iteration-loop and issue plan so I can say how this project intends to close that behavior gap.

data.text: I have a clear picture of the plan. The user wants to know HOW the project plans to fix the "don't act like Work" gap. I should explain this in human terms without dumping paths.

The project is **not rewriting Kilo or OpenCode’s engines.** It is teaching both products a selectable **Codex mode**, then scoring live chats until that mode actually produces Work’s habits. The owner says when it is close enough.

## The intended fix, in order

**1. Write the rules down from Work, not from a paper.**  
That is done. The spec says: look first, burst look, wait or send, almost never edit, no todo list, don’t bash first. Both products have a `codex` agent with those rules. CI checks the two mode files stay paired.

**2. Stop using default `code` / `build` as the exam.**  
The 8% / 16% numbers are the **old coding agents**. Those agents were never given Work’s rules. The plan is: pick **Codex mode** (Kilo’s current model, OpenCode including free build models), run work there, score **those** sessions. Right now sqlite never even stores `agent=codex`, so the loop cannot isolate “we used the mode.” That has to get fixed or the scorer stays blind.

**3. Measure, patch the mode, measure again.**  
That is issue 12, still open:

- Score a session on R1–R6 (look first, don’t write, don’t bash first, no Todowrite, don’t edit after a look burst, don’t spawn first).
- Write the gap: Kilo still look→todo→edit; OpenCode still bash-first.
- Change the **mode text** (and only if needed, routing/skills) so the next chats are less likely to do that.
- Keep both products in lockstep.
- Repeat until **you** say the harness behaves like Work.

It does **not** stop at “the markdown file looks right.” Modes already look right. Live default sessions still mutate.

**4. Then replay the same Work jobs.**  
Issue 13: take the **22 long Work threads**, feed the same asks (gitignored) into Kilo Codex mode and OpenCode as multi-turn chats. Score two things:

- Process: did it look / wait / send instead of todo+edit?
- Outcome: did it research, verify, and actually address the ask, compared with what Work did?

Develop set (16) first. Morphs (same job, warped wording) so the mode doesn’t overfit one phrasing. Holdout (6 longest) scored last, without cherry-picking mode text to those hashes.

**Stop for that slice:** all 16 develop hashes have Kilo+OpenCode process+outcome notes, at least 3 morphs, holdout scored once.

## What this will change in the product

If it works, you should notice:

- Codex mode **answers after looking** instead of opening a checklist and patching.
- Terminal is not move one.
- Multi-step work is “send this slice to X,” not six todos the same agent then implements.
- Edits become rare, and never the next click after a read burst.

The scorer’s job is to make that visible as a number (Work is **81/83**; copies should move toward that), not as a vibe.

## What it will not do

It will not swap Grok or Qwen for Codex. It will not build a third product. It will not run SWE-bench. It will not force the model at the API layer — there is no hard “block Edit after Read” in the runtime. The lever is **instructions + routing + scoring**, then you decide match.

**Where we are:** steps A–D (analysis, spec, both modes) exist. The loop is stuck on “mode written, default agents still write-happy, Codex-mode sessions not isolated.” Same-ticket replay has started on develop hashes and is not finished.
